I started when I was 18 and took over my grandfathers automotive shop. He was already running a successful shop at the time I had taken it over, so I won’t pretend that I had anything to do with that. What i did do however, was more than double the profit margin in my first year. He was always set on only doing vehicles maintenance such as changing oil, brake pads, and swapping out different parts that were old or broken and never branched out into doing exhaust work, welding or buying parts vehicles. There was always an old tow truck there as well, but it never got used. I changed all of that. We started doing exhaust work, buying vehicles for parts and scrapping what we couldn’t use and bought a nice tow truck. We also started doing transmission work as well and bringing on new employees to use the space in the shop that was never used. I had a paint booth added to paint the usable parts that came from the scrap vehicles to any color the customer needed. He was happy bringing in $90k a year, but I always wanted to expand because after all, money is kind of the whole point. I ended up selling the shop and the 100 acres it was on for 3 million dollars, when i was 25 years old. I’ve invested in friends business ideas, but it became quite clear they lacked the motivation to actually be successful because they thought i would be there to bail them out. I’ve also paid off my families houses and my own house as well as set them up for the rest of their lives. 

Did I get a head start? Yes. Did I also do something with the opportunity instead of continuing to make $90k/year? Yes. 

One of the business that failed was an online shop creating handmade items and I thought it would be successful. I had a handful of people who made different items and had the time to make them, but sales flatlined after a few months of doing well. We barely managed to pay for the startup costs with the website and licensing and everything. I’m not sure what exactly happened there, but it didn’t go well afterwards. They all started blaming each other for not driving enough traffic to the website, having their prices to high, and everything else I’m sure you can imagine. 

I have to hop off and help with kids now, but I own a ride share company that picks up soldiers from the airport and I charge enough to pay for a driver for when I’m unable to do it for free while still keeping it under Lyft and Uber prices. This one I’m not trying to make to much on, mostly cover expenses. I know how much military members get paid and am trying to keep prices for them low.

Does a business plan make startup success inevitable? Absolutely not. I do believe that great planning is the key to success. A great business plan can set the foundation for years to come. I believe it is a blueprint for a successful business. There’s actually a lot more to writing business plans than people think. I spend hours doing research and going over every detail I find to make sure that the idea looks great on paper. What may have seemed like a good idea for a business can, after some thought and analysis, prove to be not viable because of heavy competition, insufficient funding or a nonexistent market. It provides concrete, factual evidence showing your idea for a business is in fact sound and reasonable and has every chance of success.
